explanation: Fires on subword pieces inside technical names, mostly lab or clinical techniques and devices (mass spect-ROM-etry, N-MR, flow CYT-ometry, def-IBR-illator, CMR). It also fires on scattered code tokens (mysql -p, .toString, xmlns, private, #include "). Mid and weak hits are generic words in license text and medical prose.

A mixture. It fires on rare subword fragments inside unusual names and Latin or foreign terms (scala tym-pani, Aotus le-murinus, Loz-ouet, Mich-alovce, Glink-a), and on sentence ends or newlines in Russian Q&A text. It also fires on a few other-language tokens (Indonesian 'tiga', German 'Ich'). Ordinary English function words give only weak activation.

Two unrelated jobs. It fires on pig-related words (porcine, swine, pigs, pig heart) and the similar-looking 'pig' in hypopigmentation or pigments. It also fires on opening square brackets and similar markup in LaTeX or academic citation syntax ('[', ' ([@B9]', '[**', title:/author: YAML fields).

A mixture. It fires on Chinese and Japanese characters in mixed or localized text (國, 電影, 地, 推薦). It also fires on 'to' in the license phrase 'agreed to in writing', on 'but' after 'looking for a solution', and on assorted mid-sentence tokens. There is no shared trigger.

Fires on subword continuation pieces in the middle of words. The strongest are 'dig-RESS-ion', Norwegian 'art-IKK-elen', 'P-UNT-ers', REPO, 'stop-PAGE', 'CERT-IFY-ING' and 'app-ELLE-e', plus some whole words such as 'article', 'point' and 'Entry'. There is no clear semantic theme.

Mostly fires on CamelCase API or class identifiers in code (UIAlertView, NSIndexPath, UITableViewCell, currentTimeMillis, decodeURIComponent, .facebook, fwlink/?). It also fires on broken multibyte CJK/Devanagari byte tokens and on suffixes like -able, -ative and -ionic in technical prose. Overall a mixture.

Fires mainly on incomplete UTF-8 byte tokens: the first byte of a multibyte character that got split, in Chinese, Japanese, or Latin letters with diacritics such as Š, Ž, Ĉ, and Greek. Ordinary code or math tokens give weaker, occasional activation.

Fires on the letter sequence 'ir'/'Ir'/'IR' as a token, inside or at the start of words and names: Piracy, Irwin, exp-ir-atory, enc-ir-cling, Qirko, Irina, Th-ir-u-, Hepadnav-ir-idae, FLIR. Weaker on similar 'ar'/'R'/'Dir'/'Cir' tokens.

Fires on function words and numbers inside formulaic boilerplate. Examples are disclaimers ('opinions expressed ARE those of the writer'), license text ('nor', 'or copy at', 'WITHOUT WARRANTIES', 'file that accompanied') and stock notices with durations ('arrive within 8-15 days', 'respond in 36 hours'). Ordinary narrative text is weaker.

Mostly fires on structural boilerplate tokens in code and markup: Go 'package' and 'import (', HTML '<link rel', 'img src', '(string', microtime, 'Created by ... on'. It also fires on function-call parentheses in generated math problems (h(q), j(s)) and a few random prose tokens. Overall a mixture.

Fires on word-internal pieces of medical and scientific terms (endoth-EL-ium, co-AG-ulation, nyst-AG-mus, Tou-RETTE, Mel-AN-omas, amy-OT-rophic, mam-MARY). It also fires on code tokens (np.empty, CreateAssetMenu, new char[, shape=() and a few unrelated tokens.

Fires on tokens that complete a numeric time or quantity expression: the last digits of years (199[8], 200[8], 201[6]), counts (60[0], 10[0],000) and time-span nouns after numbers ('19 years', 'three decades', 'year after year', 'Gy per'). A few hits are other tokens in dated or numbered contexts.

Partly fires on blockchain, crypto and auth vocabulary (libp2p, SegWit, token_credential, off-chain, bearer, proof of work, Authorization). Partly it fires on 'of' in patent boilerplate ('by way of reference/example') and on scattered code or tech tokens. A mixture.

Mainly fires on the keyword after a declaration opener in code: TABLE/FUNCTION after CREATE, 'class' after static, typeof, import, function parameters. It also fires on the French negation 'ne'/'n'' and on assorted unrelated tokens such as version numbers and ALICE. A mixture.
